title: A provable quantum advantage for approximate optimization via decoded quantum interferometry
authors: Maximilian J. Kramer, Elies Gil-Fuster, Benjamin D. M. Jones, Jens Eisert, Franz J. Schreiber
abstract: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a novel paradigm for tackling approximate optimization problems on quantum computers. This framework comes with strong performance guarantees and exploits a well-established duality between optimization and coding theory. A central question, however, is whether DQI can actually provably outperform all polynomial-time classical algorithms. In this work, we establish such an advantage in an oracle setting: we consider an optimization task called folded optimal polynomial intersection (folded OPI), where the acceptance sets are chosen randomly and accessed through membership oracles. We establish a strict gap between the approximation ratio achievable by any polynomial-time classical algorithm and the approximation ratio achieved by the DQI algorithm. Our proof builds on Jordan et al.'s DQI framework for approximate optimization and extends the classical lower-bound method underlying Yamakawa and Zhandry's exact-search oracle separation to approximation. Building on recent developments by Sun and Wootters, Horinaga and Yamakawa, and Jo, we further show that a modified version of the DQI algorithm achieves a strictly larger gap on the folded OPI problem, yielding an even stronger quantum separation. As a concrete example, for code rate $0.3$, DQI and the modified algorithm achieve expected scores of approximately $0.85$ and $0.95$, respectively. In contrast, exceeding the classical threshold of $0.65$ by any fixed amount with constant probability on sampled instances requires super-polynomially many classical membership queries.
summary: This work proves a quantum advantage for approximate optimization by analyzing the Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) algorithm on a structured problem called folded OPI. The authors establish a strict gap between the quantum performance and the best classical performance, showing that achieving certain accuracy levels classically requires super-polynomial queries. This advances the understanding of quantum computational power in the context of structured search problems.
main_problem: The paper aims to establish a provable quantum advantage for solving approximate optimization problems using the Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) framework.
main_result: A strict separation is proven between the approximation ratio achievable by DQI and the best possible performance of any polynomial-time classical algorithm for the folded optimal polynomial intersection (folded OPI) problem.
method: The authors extend classical lower-bound methods to the approximation setting, utilizing DQI, which connects optimization to coding theory via Fourier transforms over finite fields.
model_or_system: The analysis is set in an oracle model involving membership oracles for acceptance sets, specifically applied to the folded OPI problem, which is related to coding theory structures.
key_observables: Approximation Ratio/Score ($\alpha$), Quantum Score ($\alpha_Q$), and Classical Threshold ($\alpha_C$).
important_parameters: Code Rate ($R$), Query Complexity (number of blocks $M$).
main_assumptions: The separation is established for an explicit family of balanced folded-OPI instances, and the stronger $\alpha_{fib}$ guarantee holds only on typical sampled instances.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows the approximation separation for DQI on folded OPI. Figure 2 illustrates the provable score guarantees ($\alpha_C$, $\alpha_Q$, $\alpha_{fib}$, exact search) across different rates $R$.
paper_structure: The paper builds upon Jordan et al.'s DQI framework, extends classical lower-bound methods to the approximation setting, and introduces a modified DQI algorithm achieving a stronger separation guarantee.
why_interesting: While the primary focus is quantum computation theory, the techniques involving coherent summation and state-vector analysis are highly relevant to understanding quantum measurement limitations in complex physical systems.
